newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: PRESS DIGEST - New Zealand newspapers - Feb 21.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - New Zealand newspapers - Feb 21.

text.p: Serious Fraud Office director Charles Sturt, giving evidence at the commission of inquiry into tax deals in the Cook Islands, was unable to explain on Thursday how a key Winebox deal worked. Asked by Colin Carruthers, QC, counsel assisting the Winebox Commissioner, to outline his understanding of the Magnum deal, Sturt was unable to without the help of a diagram which was among European Pacific documents. He said he found the transaction confusing and admitted to being all at sea without the diagrams. Page 1.

Maori Affairs Minister Tau Henare on Thursday referred to Aotearoa Television Network funds spent by NZ First MP Tukoroirangi Morgan on clothes as "private money". Asked by Labour MP Trevor Mallard in Parliament whether he believed Morgan had the authority to spend the taxpayer-funded station money on clothes two weeks before the election, Henare said: "As the minister of Maori affairs I have no responsibility whatsoever over what members of this House spend their own private money on." Page 2.

Treaty of Waitangi legislation that gives male Maoris in some tribes dominance should be changed because it discriminates against women, ACT NZ MP Derek Quigley said on Thursday. He told Parliament that treaty legislation gave special status to tribes that "either directly or indirectly fortifies the dominant position of males in some tribes". Page 2.

The heat has been turned up on Serious Fraud Office head Charles Sturt, with Prime Minister Jim Bolger saying it was unacceptable for a senior public servant to knowingly mislead a minister. Alliance leader Jim Anderton has called for Sturt's resignation after his admission to the Cook Islands tax commission of inquiry that a 1994 statement to Attorney-General Paul East, in which he said the office had investigated the Winebox documents and found no evidence of fraud, was not "strictly" correct. Page 2.

New Zealand's third largest life insurance company, NZI Life, is up for sale but parent company General Accident will keep its NZI fire and general business in New Zealand. Sir Ron Brierley's Guinness Peat Group, AMP Society and Prudential have been touted as potential buyers but all three refused to comment on Thursday. The sale is expected to be completed by the end of next month. Page 13.

Property for Industry plans to spend up to $30 million on new investments in the current financial year, taking its portfolio to a fully invested $150 million. PFI on Thursday reported a tax paid profit of $5.29 million, up only marginally on the $5.19 million for the previous year. Page 13.

Wellington business should be better during the next 12 months, but only because companies are expecting interest rates and the dollar to keep falling, according to a survey. The Wellington Regional Chamber of Commerce survey of members shows an expected upturn, after a drop in activity between December 1995 and last December. Page 13.

Fletcher Challenge Energy said on Thursday that drilling at its Mangahewa-2 well had confirmed its estimates of gas-bearing structures and saturations. The formation is known to contain large amounts of gas, though extraction poses technical difficulties that involve fracturing rock. A Fletcher spokesman said the success of the field depended not on how much gas was there, but on how much could be got out. "We're not going to know that until we have done the fracturing," he said. Page 13.

New Zealand's largest sharebroker, First NZ Capital, is advising clients to downgrade their positions in New Zealand bonds and equities. The view, published in a strategy review issued to clients, comes in the middle of a company reporting season that disappointed many analysts and is in contrast to a rosy market outlook painted by many analysts at the start of the year. First NZ Capital is recommending that investors increase their holding in cash. Page 13.

A review of the way inflation was measured would consider removing housing from the consumer price index, Statistics Minister Maurice Williamson said on Thursday. Williamson told Parliament that the review of the methods for measuring the CPI would be carried out in May, with a report expected in July. Page 13.
